summary: This USDA Economic Research Service page examines drought in the western United States and its effects on agriculture. It explains how the U.S. Drought Monitor classifies drought and reports that conditions as of April 4, 2023 had improved compared with 2021 and 2022, though the summer of 2021 was historically severe. It highlights alfalfa hay impacts and lists ERS outlook reports, state fact sheets, publications and charts on drought-related topics.
one_line: USDA ERS page on western U.S. drought conditions as of April 2023 and their impacts on agriculture, with links to related reports.
key_facts: The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) categorizes drought on a scale from D0 (Abnormally Dry) to D4 (Exceptional Drought), based on soil moisture, streamflow, and precipitation levels.
As of April 4, 2023, drought conditions had improved across much of the western United States compared to 2021 and 2022.

The note defines the 17 western States as Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming.
Conditions were most severe in Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, and Oregon as of April 2023.
On April 4, 2023, 12 percent of land in western states was classified as experiencing extreme or exceptional drought, with an additional 20 percent classified as severe.
Data reported by USDM show that drought incidence in the western United States during the summer of 2021 exceeded all past droughts in the region since 2000.
Significant precipitation over the 2022–23 winter reduced the prevalence of drought in many western states.

As of April 4, 2023, approximately 12 percent of alfalfa hay acreage in the United States was experiencing severe, extreme, or exceptional drought, according to the National Drought Mitigation Center (NDMC).
Alfalfa hay acreage affected by severe or worse drought peaked at 52 percent in August of 2021.
Alfalfa hay is an important input for livestock and dairy operations, so drought-related reductions in its yields may influence feed and consumer prices.
Drought can diminish crop and livestock outputs in rainfall-dependent regions and may severely affect farm profitability.
Drought reduces snowpack and streamflow available for diversions to irrigated agricultural land.
The page was last updated on Friday, February 09, 2024, and the contact listed is Aaron Hrozencik.
